fixes.explanation: Sadness is a fair guess, friend, but James uses a different word. He says "…there will be disorder and every evil practice." Sadness at least sounds tidy. Disorder is the opposite of tidy, and I've dropped enough cookie sheets to know.

Yes, baker. James says "Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness." They sow in peace, and the fruit of righteousness is what they reap. It's the opposite of the disorder he just warned about.
James doesn't say regret here, friend. He says "Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness." What the peacemakers reap is the fruit of righteousness, and regret isn't in the verse.

True, baker. James asks, "What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don’t they come from the passions at war within you?" He points inside them, not at somebody else. The passions at war within are where he looks for the source.

James does say they ask, friend, but quitting early isn't the reason he gives. He says, "…you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures." The reason he names is their motives.

Yes, baker. James says "…friendship with the world is hostility toward God?" I think that's strong language. He follows it with "…whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God."

James actually says it the other way around, friend. He says, "Turn your laughter to mourning, and your joy to gloom." So laughter turns into mourning, not the reverse. I think this one is a heavy word.

James doesn't put it that way, friend. He says the one Lawgiver and Judge is "…the One who is able to save and destroy." Build and plant sounds like a landscaping crew, but those aren't the words in the verse. The words are save and destroy.

Those are good words, baker, but they aren't James's. He says, "There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and destroy." The words are save and destroy. Then he asks, "But who are you to judge your neighbor?"
